text.p: Fabri-Centers of America Inc has agreed to repay $3.28 million in proceeds from securities sales to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges that it inflated its earnings, the SEC said Tuesday.

In the settlement, disclosed simultaneously with the filing of a civil complaint by the SEC in U.S. District Court here, the company also accepted a court order barring it from further violations of securities laws, the agency said.
Fabri-Centers did not admit or deny the SEC charges, the agency said.
The SEC alleged that Fabri-Centers and two former officers materially overstated the company's earnings and profitability in public documents for fiscal 1992, ended February 1, 1992.

In the public documents, the company deviated from its prior accounting practice, erroneously calculated a key inventory reserve, and failed to disclose heightened price competition, the agency alleged.

By overstating its earnings, the company was able to sell $74.75 million in convertible debt in March 1992 at better prices and on more favorable terms than if it had provided accurate information, the SEC alleged.

The two former corporate executives, former Chief Financial Officer Robert Norton and former Comptroller Joseph Williams, did not agree to settle charges that they circumvented the company's internal accounting controls and that Norton made false and misleading statements to auditors about the offering, it said.
The SEC said it is moving ahead with civil litigation against Norton and Williams before U.S. District Court Judge Harold Greene.

Norton's lawyers, Stanley Arkin and John Sturc, issued a statement calling the complaint an "unjustified dispute over the application of accounting principles" and said the SEC could not present evidence that Norton committed any violations.

"Rather, the evidence will show that Norton and his subordinates carefully applied the correct accounting principles and caused Fabri-Centers to make prompt and accurate disclosures," the attorneys said.

Charges against the company also included making material false public statements in May and June 1992, violating anti-fraud provisions of federal securities laws, and violating reporting, record-keeping and internal controls provisions.

The SEC said it also simultaneously brought and settled charges against Alan Rosskamm, the current chairman and chief executive officer of the Hudson, Ohio-based operator of retail, fabric and crafts stores.

Without admitting or denying the charges, the agency said Rosskamm consented to findings that he violated securities laws by failing to make adequate inquiries before signing off on letters to the company's independent auditors and by signing and approving company documents filed with the SEC.
